claim: Coronary artery disease is the leading cause of death worldwide.
source: Coronary artery disease is the leading cause of death worldwide, but there is currently no effective method to regenerate new coronary arteries (CA) in diseased or injured hearts (Rubanyi, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rubanyi, 2013

claim: There is currently no effective method to regenerate new coronary arteries in diseased or injured hearts.
source: Coronary artery disease is the leading cause of death worldwide, but there is currently no effective method to regenerate new coronary arteries (CA) in diseased or injured hearts (Rubanyi, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rubanyi, 2013

claim: Coronary arteries are vessels that supply blood to ventricular heart muscle.
source: CAs are the vessels that supply blood to ventricular heart muscle and are composed of an inner endothelial cell lining wrapped by a smooth muscle covering.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about coronary artery anatomy and function

claim: Coronary arteries are composed of an inner endothelial cell lining wrapped by a smooth muscle covering.
source: CAs are the vessels that supply blood to ventricular heart muscle and are composed of an inner endothelial cell lining wrapped by a smooth muscle covering.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about coronary artery structure

claim: Coronary artery smooth muscle cells play an important role in the pathogenesis of coronary artery disease.
source: Coronary artery smooth muscle cells (caSMC) are particularly important due to their role in the pathogenesis of coronary artery disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cardiovascular disease research

claim: caSMC development is a poorly understood process.
source: However, caSMC development, both normally during embryogenesis and ectopically during coronary artery disease, is a poorly understood process.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field

claim: CaSMC development occurs during arterialization of immature coronary plexus vessels.
source: CaSMC development occurs during arterialization of immature coronary plexus vessels.
evidence: This is established knowledge about coronary development

claim: Coronary endothelial cells are derived primarily from the sinus venosus and endocardial cells.
source: In the murine heart, coronary endothelial cells derived primarily from the sinus venosus and endocardial cells that sprout onto the heart to form an early vascular plexus (Kattan et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2014b; Red-Horse et al., 2010; Tian et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Coronary endothelial cells sprout onto the heart to form an early vascular plexus.
source: In the murine heart, coronary endothelial cells derived primarily from the sinus venosus and endocardial cells that sprout onto the heart to form an early vascular plexus (Kattan et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2014b; Red-Horse et al., 2010; Tian et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: A subset of plexus vessels differentiates into arteries once the network attaches to the aorta and begins receiving blood flow.
source: A subset of the plexus vessels differentiates into arteries once the network attaches to the aorta and begins receiving blood flow (Chen et al, 2014a; Hood et al., 1992; Peeters et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The source of caSMCs is different from coronary artery endothelial cells.
source: Although ultimately adjacent to CA endothelial cells, the source of caSMCs is different.
evidence: This is established knowledge about coronary development

claim: caSMCs arise from the epicardium.
source: These cells arise from the mesothelial covering of the heart called the epicardium (Cai et al., 2008b; Mikawa and Gourdie, 1996; Wilm et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: In rodents, caSMCs reside deep within the myocardium while epicardial cells are located on the outermost layer of the heart.
source: In rodents, caSMCs reside deep within the myocardium while epicardial cells are located on the outermost layer of the heart.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge

claim: During embryonic development, many epicardial cells undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and migrate into the deeper layers of the myocardium.
source: During embryonic development, many epicardial cells undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and migrate into the deeper layers of the myocardium to form the stromal cells of the heart, including cardiac fibroblasts and caSMCs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about epicardial cell behavior during development

claim: Epicardial cells form the stromal cells of the heart, including cardiac fibroblasts and caSMCs.
source: During embryonic development, many epicardial cells undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and migrate into the deeper layers of the myocardium to form the stromal cells of the heart, including cardiac fibroblasts and caSMCs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about epicardial cell differentiation

claim: Deletion of Platelet Derived Growth Factor Receptor β (PDGFRβ) diminishes caSMC development.
source: Inhibition of epicardial migration from the surface by deletion of Platelet Derived Growth Factor Receptor β (PDGFRβ) diminishes caSMC development (Mellgren, et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mellgren et al., 2008 and Smith et al., 2011

claim: The migrating epicardial-derived cell type fated to become caSMCs has not been discovered.
source: However, the migrating epicardial-derived cell type fated to become caSMCs has not been discovered, and the mechanisms that trigger this intermediate progenitor to differentiate into caSMCs are unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study

claim: The mechanisms that trigger the intermediate progenitor to differentiate into caSMCs are unknown.
source: However, the migrating epicardial-derived cell type fated to become caSMCs has not been discovered, and the mechanisms that trigger this intermediate progenitor to differentiate into caSMCs are unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study

claim: Smooth muscle within other internal organs arises from an outer mesothelial covering.
source: Smooth muscle within other internal organs, including vascular smooth muscle, also arises from an outer mesothelial covering.
evidence: This is established knowledge about smooth muscle development

claim: Lineage tracing Mesothelin (Msln)-positive mesothelial cells has shown that many of the abdominal and thoracic organs derive their smooth muscle and fibroblasts from the surface serosa layer.
source: Lineage tracing Mesothelin (Msln)-positive mesothelial cells and their prospective isolation and transplantation has shown that many of the abdominal and thoracic organs derive their smooth muscle and fibroblasts from the surface serosa layer (Rinkevich et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rinkevich et al., 2012

claim: Mesothelial to vascular smooth muscle differentiation occurred almost exclusively during developmental and early postnatal stages.
source: Mesothelial to vascular smooth muscle differentiation occurred almost exclusively during developmental and early postnatal stages, but, similar to the heart, the cellular pathway bridging the surface to internal arteries has not been identified.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies

claim: The cellular pathway bridging the surface to internal arteries has not been identified.
source: Mesothelial to vascular smooth muscle differentiation occurred almost exclusively during developmental and early postnatal stages, but, similar to the heart, the cellular pathway bridging the surface to internal arteries has not been identified.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study

claim: Epicardial mesothelium of the heart has a developmental restriction.
source: Epicardial mesothelium of the heart also has a developmental restriction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about epicardial development

claim: Most migrating caSMC progenitors leave the heart surface before embryonic day 12.5.
source: Most migrating caSMC progenitors leave the heart surface before embryonic day 12.5 and are no longer able to migrate into the adult heart, either normally or following myocardial infarction (Wei et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wei et al., 2015 and Zhou et al., 2011

claim: Epicardial cells are no longer able to migrate into the adult heart, either normally or following myocardial infarction.
source: Most migrating caSMC progenitors leave the heart surface before embryonic day 12.5 and are no longer able to migrate into the adult heart, either normally or following myocardial infarction (Wei et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wei et al., 2015 and Zhou et al., 2011

claim: Cells resembling vascular pericytes are intermediate progenitors for smooth muscle in the developing heart.
source: Here, we find that cells resembling vascular pericytes (PDGFRβ+Notch3+NG2+SM-MHC−SMα−PDGFRα−, wrapping microvessels, embedded within a basement membrane) are intermediate progenitors for smooth muscle in the developing heart.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experimental approaches described in the manuscript

claim: Pericytes are mural cells that wrap microvascular blood vessels and regulate their development and function.
source: Pericytes are mural cells that wrap microvascular blood vessels and regulate their development and function (Armulik et al., 2011; Cappellari et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Armulik et al., 2011 and Cappellari et al., 2013

claim: Pericytes share features with smooth muscle cells including close apposition to the vessel and some molecular markers.
source: Pericytes share features with smooth muscle cells including close apposition to the vessel and some molecular markers, but differ in their contractile protein expression, cell shape, location on capillaries instead of large vessels, and discontinuous covering of the endothelium.
evidence: This is established knowledge about pericyte characteristics

claim: Pericytes differ from smooth muscle cells in their contractile protein expression, cell shape, location on capillaries instead of large vessels, and discontinuous covering of the endothelium.
source: Pericytes share features with smooth muscle cells including close apposition to the vessel and some molecular markers, but differ in their contractile protein expression, cell shape, location on capillaries instead of large vessels, and discontinuous covering of the endothelium.
evidence: This is established knowledge about pericyte characteristics

claim: Pericytes were first identified in 1873.
source: Since their identification in 1873 (Rouget, 1873), biologists have wondered whether pericytes and smooth muscle differentiate into each other, but direct evidence has been lacking (Armulik et al., 2011; Cappellari et al., 2013; Majesky, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rouget, 1873

claim: Biologists have wondered whether pericytes and smooth muscle differentiate into each other, but direct evidence has been lacking.
source: Since their identification in 1873 (Rouget, 1873), biologists have wondered whether pericytes and smooth muscle differentiate into each other, but direct evidence has been lacking (Armulik et al., 2011; Cappellari et al., 2013; Majesky, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Armulik et al., 2011, Cappellari et al., 2013, and Majesky, 2011

claim: Pericytes lining the coronary vascular plexus respond to Notch3 signaling at arterial remodeling zones to become mature caSMCs during embryonic development.
source: We provide evidence that pericytes lining the coronary vascular plexus respond to Notch3 signaling at arterial remodeling zones to become mature caSMCs during embryonic development.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data including Notch3 mutant analysis

claim: caSMC related pericytes are present in the adult heart.
source: We also observed caSMC related pericytes in the adult heart presenting the possibility that the Notch3 pathway could be manipulated in these cells to participate in CA regeneration.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by clonal analysis data in adult hearts

claim: SM-MHClow cells were on average 50 µm deep from the epicardium.
source: Measuring the distance between SM-MHClow cells and the epicardium revealed that they were not on the surface of the heart, but on average 50 µm deep (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by distance measurements shown in Figure 1H

claim: A putative intermediate progenitor would need to migrate through approximately 7 cell layers between the epicardium and nascent CAs.
source: Thus, a putative intermediate progenitor would need to migrate through approximately 7 cell layers between the epicardium and nascent CAs where they first express the mature smooth muscle cell marker (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is inferred from the distance measurements and cell size estimates

claim: Tbx18-Cre induces recombination in the large majority of epicardial cells.
source: Tbx18-Cre was selected because, in control experiments with other Cre reporters, recombination was induced in the large majority of epicardial cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Clones containing epicardial cells and caSMCs always contained sister cells with long, thread-like processes that wrapped around coronary vessels.
source: Initial experiments analyzing Tbx18-Cre, MADM clones based on cellular morphology and location revealed that clones containing epicardial cells and caSMCs always contained sister cells with long, thread-like processes that wrapped around coronary vessels (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Sister cells from clones that were adjacent to, but did not incorporate into, the caSMC layer, were mostly located in the space between vessels instead of wrapping around them.
source: This was in contrast to sister cells from clones that were adjacent to, but did not incorporate into, the caSMC layer, which were mostly located in the space between vessels instead of wrapping around them (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 2B

claim: CaSMCs were positive for SM-MHC and PDGFRβ and were around mature and developing arteries.
source: CaSMCs were positive for SM-MHC and PDGFRβ and were around mature and developing arteries (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2C

claim: PDGFRβ perivascular cells around microvessels were SM-MHC negative.
source: In contrast, PDGFRβ perivascular cells around microvessels were SM-MHC negative (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2C

claim: SMα immunolabeling was only in larger, more proximal CAs, and not in PDGFRβ+ cells around plexus capillaries.
source: Aside from a low level in some cardiomyocytes, SMα immunolabeling was only in larger, more proximal CAs, and not in PDGFRβ+ cells around plexus capillaries (Figure 2D) or in SM-MHC+ cells in smaller vessels and remodeling zones (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D and 2E

claim: In the coronary system, SMα appeared to be induced later than SM-MHC since its expression domain was less extensive and only in more mature arteries.
source: Thus, in the coronary system, SMα appeared to be induced later than SM-MHC since its expression domain was less extensive and only in more mature arteries.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunostaining patterns observed in Figures 2D and 2E

claim: CNN1 was highly expressed in cardiomyocytes, but did not appear in intervening PDGFRβ+ cells.
source: CNN1 was highly expressed in cardiomyocytes, but did not appear in intervening PDGFRβ+ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: Around large coronary arteries a subset of caSMCs expressed CNN1.
source: Around large coronary arteries a subset of caSMCs expressed CNN1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: PDGFRβ+ cells surrounding plexus capillaries in the free walls of the developing heart ventricles were always closely apposed to endothelial cells.
source: Whole mount immunohistochemistry showed that PDGFRβ+ cells surrounding plexus capillaries in the free walls of the developing heart ventricles were always closely apposed to endothelial cells in contrast to PDGFRα+ fibroblasts, which were dispersed between the endothelium (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B

claim: PDGFRα+ fibroblasts were dispersed between the endothelium.
source: Whole mount immunohistochemistry showed that PDGFRβ+ cells surrounding plexus capillaries in the free walls of the developing heart ventricles were always closely apposed to endothelial cells in contrast to PDGFRα+ fibroblasts, which were dispersed between the endothelium (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B

claim: PDGFRβ+ cells were embedded within a Collagen IV-containing basement membrane.
source: PDGFRβ+ cells were also embedded within a Collagen IV-containing basement membrane (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 3C,D

claim: PDGFRβ+ cells all expressed the pericyte markers NG2 and Notch3.
source: They also all expressed the pericyte markers NG2 (Figure 2I) and Notch3 (Figure 2J) (Liu et al., 2010) (quantification shown in Figure 2K).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2I, 2J, and quantification in Figure 2K

claim: PDGFRβ+ cells were observed on the earliest coronary sprouts when the vessels first migrate directly beneath the epicardium.
source: PDGFRβ+ cells were observed on the earliest coronary sprouts when the vessels first migrate directly beneath the epicardium and surrounded the entire plexus endothelium as it developed (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: At the arterial remodeling zone where caSMCs first differentiate, 98% of PDGFRβ+ cells were Tbx18-Cre lineage labeled.
source: Later, at the arterial remodeling zone where caSMCs first differentiate, 98 ± % of PDGFRβ+ cells were Tbx18-Cre lineage labeled consistent with most arising from the epicardium (Figure 2K).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing quantification shown in Figure 2K

claim: PDGFRβ+ cells were the most numerous Tbx18-Cre traced cell type at the arterial remodeling zone.
source: In addition, PDGFRβ+ cells were the most numerous Tbx18-Cre traced cell type in this location (Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 5A

claim: The remaining 28% of Tbx18-Cre traced cells at the arterial remodeling zone were predominately fibroblasts.
source: The remaining 28% were predominately fibroblasts as defined by their expression of PDGFRα and variable proximity to the vessels (Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: Supported by quantification and immunostaining data shown in Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 5B

claim: Much of the coronary smooth muscle was lineage labeled with Tbx18-Cre at time points after arteries are formed.
source: At time points after arteries are formed, much of the coronary smooth muscle was also lineage labeled with Tbx18-Cre (Figure 2M) in line with other studies showing an epicardial origin for these cells (Cai et al., 2008b; Wilm et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 2M and citations to previous studies

claim: PDGFRβ cells did not overlap with CD45 staining.
source: The epicardium is not thought to give rise to cells of the hematopoietic lineage, and, accordingly, PDGFRβ cells did not overlap with CD45 staining (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data (not shown in manuscript)

claim: Greater than 80% of the observed clusters were truly clonal.
source: This analysis revealed that ∼82% of the observed clusters were likely to derive from a single labeling event (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by mathematical modeling shown in Figure 3B

claim: At e13.5 before caSMCs are present, clones consisted of just epicardial cells and pericytes.
source: At e13.5 before caSMCs are present, we obtained clones consisting of just epicardial cells and pericytes, the latter of which were always located directly beneath epicardial sister cells (Figure 3D-e13.5, E).
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 3D-e13.5 and Figure 3E

claim: At e15.5, clones with caSMCs always contained pericytes that filled the region of the myocardium between the epicardium and smooth muscle.
source: At e15.5, clones with caSMCs always contained pericytes that filled the region of the myocardium between the epicardium and smooth muscle and were continuous with, and often touching, related caSMCs (Figure 3D-e15.5, E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B, and Videos 1,2).
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 3D-e15.5, Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B, and Videos 1,2

claim: Pericytes were the most numerous cell type in e15.5 clones.
source: As expected from the Tbx18-Cre lineage trace data (Figure 2L), pericytes were the most numerous cell type in these clones (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C

claim: Tbx18-Cre labels cardiomyocytes, but these cells never appeared in clonal clusters with pericytes or smooth muscle.
source: Tbx18-Cre labels cardiomycytes (Cai et al., 2008b), but these cells never appeared in clonal clusters with pericytes or smooth muscle.
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data and citation to Cai et al., 2008b

claim: Adult Tbx18-Cre, MADM hearts frequently contained tightly packed clusters of lineage labeled cells consisting of pericytes and caSMCs.
source: Strikingly, adult Tbx18-Cre, MADM hearts frequently contained tightly packed clusters of lineage labeled cells consisting of pericytes and caSMCs (Figure 3D-adult) (n = 20).
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data in adult hearts shown in Figure 3D-adult

claim: Adult pericytes exhibited even longer, thinner processes that tracked along the vessels for greater than 5–10 times the length of their cell bodies.
source: Pericytes at this stage exhibited even longer, thinner processes that tracked along the vessels for greater than 5–10 times the length of their cell bodies (Figure 3D-adult and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3D-adult and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D

claim: Pericytes and caSMCs do not migrate significantly once their positions are established during development.
source: The fact that these cells were not dispersed, even five weeks after labeling, shows that pericytes and caSMCs do not migrate significantly once their positions are established during development.
evidence: This is inferred from the tight clustering of labeled cells in adult hearts

claim: Within established adult clones, the ratio between the number of pericytes and caSMCs was comparable to ratios calculated for total mural cells from three different regions of the heart.
source: Within established adult clones, the ratio between the number of pericytes and caSMCs was comparable to ratios calculated for total mural cells from three different regions of the heart (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3F

claim: NG2- and Notch3-positive cells on the microvasculature always expressed PDGFRβ and wrapped vessels.
source: In the myocardium of the developing ventricle free walls, NG2- and Notch3-positive cells on the microvasculature always expressed PDGFRβ and wrapped vessels (Figure 2I–K), which identified them as cardiac pericytes (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2I-K

claim: NG2 and Notch3 completely overlapped.
source: NG2 and Notch3 also completely overlapped (n = 185 cells counted, data not shown).
evidence: Supported by cell counting data (not shown in manuscript)

claim: Cre recombination efficiency in PDGFRβ+SM-MHC- perivascular cells (pericytes) was 21% with NG2-CreER.
source: Quantifying the proportion of lineage labeled pericytes in the compact myocardium indicated that Cre recombination efficiency in PDGFRβ+SM-MHC- perivascular cells (pericytes) was 21% and 38% with NG2-CreER and Notch3-CreER, respectively (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Cre recombination efficiency in PDGFRβ+SM-MHC- perivascular cells (pericytes) was 38% with Notch3-CreER.
source: Quantifying the proportion of lineage labeled pericytes in the compact myocardium indicated that Cre recombination efficiency in PDGFRβ+SM-MHC- perivascular cells (pericytes) was 21% and 38% with NG2-CreER and Notch3-CreER, respectively (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4D

claim: SM-MHC+ caSMCs expressed the tdtomato lineage label in both NG2-CreER and Notch3-CreER strains.
source: SM-MHC+ caSMCs also expressed the tdtomato lineage label in both NG2-CreER (Figure 4E,F) and Notch3-CreER (Figure 4G,H) strains.
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 4E,F,G,H

claim: Similar percentages of labeling were seen in pericytes and caSMC consistent with low recombination efficiencies in pericytes accounting for the incomplete caSMC tracing.
source: Similar percentages of labeling were seen in pericytes and caSMC (quantified in the compact myocardium) consistent with low recombination efficiencies in pericytes accounting for the incomplete caSMC tracing (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Both NG2-CreER and Notch3-CreER transgenes exhibited sporadic labeling in cardiomyocytes.
source: One potential confounding factor is that both transgenes exhibited sporadic labeling in cardiomyocytes (Ozerdem et al., 2001), which was more rare in Notch3-CreER (Figure 4E,G).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 4E,G and citation to Ozerdem et al., 2001

claim: Cardiomyocyte lineage tracing never labeled caSMCs.
source: However, control experiments using Myh6-CreER showed that cardiomyocyte lineage tracing never labeled caSMCs (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by control lineage tracing experiments (data not shown)

claim: PDGFRβ-null mice have reduced caSMCs.
source: PDGFRβ-null mice have reduced caSMCs (Figure 5A) (Hellström et al., 1999; Smith et al., 2011); however, they undergo vascular remodeling exhibiting a recognizable arterial remodeling zone and CA (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A and citations to Hellström et al., 1999 and Smith et al., 2011

claim: PDGFRβ-null mice undergo vascular remodeling exhibiting a recognizable arterial remodeling zone and CA.
source: PDGFRβ-null mice have reduced caSMCs (Figure 5A) (Hellström et al., 1999; Smith et al., 2011); however, they undergo vascular remodeling exhibiting a recognizable arterial remodeling zone and CA (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Notch3+ pericytes at the remodeling zone were significantly decreased in PDGFRβ-null mice.
source: Analyzing the total number of Notch3+ pericytes at the remodeling zone revealed that they were significantly decreased (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5B,C

claim: Pericytes and caSMCs were not completely gone in PDGFRβ-null mice suggesting the presence of a very inefficient compensatory mechanism.
source: Pericytes and caSMCs were not completely gone (Figure 5B,C) suggesting the presence of a very inefficient compensatory mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some pericytes and caSMCs remain in PDGFRβ-null mice

claim: Notch3 was upregulated in pericytes at the region where SM-MHC protein expression was initiated.
source: Among those investigated, Notch3 was upregulated in pericytes at the region where SM-MHC protein expression was initiated (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6A,B

claim: The arterial remodeling zone can be identified based on Notch3 staining intensity without visualizing vessel structure.
source: In fact, the arterial remodeling zone can be identified based on Notch3 staining intensity without visualizing vessel structure (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A

claim: PDGFRβ was uniformly expressed in mural cells throughout the vasculature.
source: This pattern was in contrast to PDGFRβ, which was uniformly expressed in mural cells throughout the vasculature (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6A,B

claim: Jagged-1 is expressed in arterial endothelium and stimulates smooth muscle differentiation including inducing the expression of SM-MHC.
source: Jagged-1 has been shown to be a major ligand for Notch3 in other organs, where it is expressed in arterial endothelium and stimulates smooth muscle differentiation including inducing the expression of SM-MHC (Briot et al., 2014; Doi et al., 2006; High et al., 2008; Hofmann et al., 2012; Jin et al., 2008; Kofler et al., 2011; Manderfield et al., 2012; Yang and Proweller, 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: High levels of Jagged-1 were specifically expressed at arterial remodeling zones where SM-MHC+ cells were developing and in CAs.
source: We found high levels of Jagged-1 to be specifically expressed at arterial remodeling zones where SM-MHC+ cells were developing and in CAs (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Jagged-1 has been identified as a shear stress-induced molecule in vitro.
source: Given that Jagged-1 has previously been identified as a shear stress-induced molecule in vitro (McCormick et al., 2001), we investigated whether it could be regulated by blood flow in the heart.
evidence: Supported by citation to McCormick et al., 2001

claim: Coronary vessels are initially unperfused, but begin to receive blood flow after they attach to the aorta at e13.5.
source: Coronary vessels are initially unperfused, but begin to receive blood flow after they attach to the aorta at e13.5 (Chen et al., 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2014a

claim: The onset of blood flow at e13.5 correlated with the onset of robust Jagged-1 expression in endothelial cells of vessels directly downstream of the attachment site.
source: This time point correlated with the onset of robust Jagged-1 expression in endothelial cells of vessels directly downstream of the attachment site (Figure 6D–WT and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Jagged-1 was only upregulated in arterial remodeling zones of e13.5 Isl1 mutant hearts that had formed CA stems on the aorta to receive blood flow.
source: Immunostaining Isl1 mutant hearts revealed that Jagged-1 was only upregulated in arterial remodeling zones of e13.5 hearts that had formed CA stems on the aorta to receive blood flow (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D,E

claim: Isl1 mutant hearts failed to upregulate Notch3 in pericytes.
source: Isl1 mutant hearts also failed to upregulate Notch3 in pericytes suggesting that this change also requires signals downstream of blood flow (n = 9, data not shown).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data (not shown in manuscript)

claim: CAs in Notch3-null mice displayed significantly reduced levels of SM-MHC when compared to controls at e15.5 and e17.5.
source: CAs in Notch3-null mice displayed significantly reduced levels of SM-MHC when compared to controls at two time points examined, e15.5 and e17.5 (Figure 7A,B and data not shown).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 7A,B

claim: SMα was reduced in Notch3-null mice.
source: SMα was also reduced (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7C

claim: CA coverage by PDGFRβ- cells was similar to wild type counterparts in Notch3-null mice.
source: In contrast, CA coverage by PDGFRβ- cells was similar to wild type counterparts (Figure 7D), and PDGFRβ staining revealed that pericytes were still present in normal numbers in the absence of Notch3 (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 7D,E

claim: Pericytes were still present in normal numbers in the absence of Notch3.
source: In contrast, CA coverage by PDGFRβ- cells was similar to wild type counterparts (Figure 7D), and PDGFRβ staining revealed that pericytes were still present in normal numbers in the absence of Notch3 (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 7D,E

claim: Quantification of EdU+ mural cells (PDGFRβ+) showed no difference between wild type and Notch3 knockout genotypes.
source: We next used EdU labeling to mark cycling cells in wildtype and knockout hearts. Quantification of EdU+ mural cells (PDGFRβ+) showed no difference between the two genotypes (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation and quantification data shown in Figure 7F

claim: Epicardial to pericyte differentiation and arterial coverage is not severely affected in Notch3-null mice.
source: Thus, epicardial to pericyte differentiation and arterial coverage is not severely affected, but caSMC maturation, specifically the induction of contractile proteins (SM-MHC and SMα), is disrupted (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that pericyte numbers are normal but contractile protein expression is reduced in Notch3-null mice

claim: caSMC maturation, specifically the induction of contractile proteins (SM-MHC and SMα), is disrupted in Notch3-null mice.
source: Thus, epicardial to pericyte differentiation and arterial coverage is not severely affected, but caSMC maturation, specifically the induction of contractile proteins (SM-MHC and SMα), is disrupted (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing reduced SM-MHC and SMα in Notch3-null mice

claim: Coronary vessels upregulate Jagged-1 after attaching to the aorta to receive arterial blood flow.
source: These data show that coronary vessels upregulate Jagged-1 after attaching to the aorta to receive arterial blood flow, and that Notch3 is required for pericyte to caSMCs differentiation, possibly in response to Jagged-1 expression at the arterial remodeling zone.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in wild type and Isl1 mutant hearts

claim: Notch3 is required for pericyte to caSMCs differentiation.
source: These data show that coronary vessels upregulate Jagged-1 after attaching to the aorta to receive arterial blood flow, and that Notch3 is required for pericyte to caSMCs differentiation, possibly in response to Jagged-1 expression at the arterial remodeling zone.
evidence: Supported by analysis of Notch3-null mice showing disrupted caSMC differentiation

claim: SM-MHC+ cells first appear at e14 on developing intralobular arteries in the kidney.
source: Characterization of smooth muscle development in the kidney using whole mount confocal microscopy showed that SM-MHC+ cells first appear at e14 on developing intralobular arteries (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8A

claim: NG2 labels pericytes in the developing kidney.
source: As in the heart, NG2 also labels pericytes in the developing kidney (Lin et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin et al., 2008

claim: Both NG2-CreER and Notch3-CreER lineage tracing resulted in robust lineage labeling of arterial smooth muscle cells in the kidney at e15.5.
source: Both approaches resulted in robust lineage labeling of arterial smooth muscle cells in the kidney at e15.5 as well as other perivascular cells including those within the glomerulus (Figure 8C and data not shown).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 8C

claim: Pericytes form an intermediate stage during smooth muscle differentiation in the kidney.
source: Although understanding the precise cellular pathway from mesothelium to smooth muscle requires further study, these data suggest that, similar to the heart, pericytes form an intermediate stage during this differentiation process in the kidney.
evidence: This is inferred from the lineage tracing data showing that NG2+ and Notch3+ cells give rise to smooth muscle in the kidney

claim: This is the first demonstration that pericytes are progenitors for smooth muscle.
source: Our data are the first demonstration that pericytes are progenitors for smooth muscle, and their presence in adult hearts reveals a new potential cell type for targeting during cardiovascular disease.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the primary finding of the study

claim: The presence of pericytes in adult hearts reveals a new potential cell type for targeting during cardiovascular disease.
source: Our data are the first demonstration that pericytes are progenitors for smooth muscle, and their presence in adult hearts reveals a new potential cell type for targeting during cardiovascular disease.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications based on the findings

claim: Previous identification of the epicardial-derived caSMC progenitor had been hampered by the fact that multiple developmental pathways occur downstream of epicardial differentiation.
source: Previous identification of the epicardial-derived caSMC progenitor had been hampered by the fact that multiple developmental pathways occur downstream of epicardial differentiation.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in the field prior to this study

claim: Clonal analysis of epicardial-derived cells identified cells with the molecular marker and morphological profile of vascular pericytes as being lineage related to caSMCs.
source: Our clonal analysis of epicardial-derived cells identified cells with the molecular marker and morphological profile of vascular pericytes as being lineage related to caSMCs.
evidence: This is a summary of the clonal analysis findings

claim: The temporal presence and position of pericytes in epicardial-derived clones suggested that pericytes were the intermediate differentiation step between the epicardium and smooth muscle.
source: The temporal presence and position of pericytes in epicardial-derived clones suggested that pericytes were the intermediate differentiation step between the epicardium and smooth muscle.
evidence: This is inferred from the clonal analysis data showing the spatial and temporal arrangement of cell types

claim: Pericytes were the most numerous epicardial-derived cell type at the CA remodeling zone where they wrapped developing arteries.
source: In addition, pericytes were the most numerous epicardial-derived cell type at the CA remodeling zone where they wrapped developing arteries, a location that would allow them to respond to arterial maturation signals.
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2L

claim: Upon attachment to the aorta and establishment of blood flow, coronary endothelial cells downstream of the attachment site induce Jagged-1.
source: We found that upon attachment to the aorta and establishment of blood flow, coronary endothelial cells downstream of the attachment site, which presumably receive the strongest blood flow, induce Jagged-1.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in wild type and Isl1 mutant hearts

claim: Jagged-1 was not robustly expressed in a model of delayed aortic attachment and delayed initiation of blood flow.
source: Jagged-1 was not robustly expressed in a model of delayed aortic attachment and delayed initiation of blood flow.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Isl1 mutant hearts

claim: Notch3 was upregulated in pericytes at the arterial remodeling zone.
source: The Jagged-1 ligand Notch3 was upregulated in pericytes at the arterial remodeling zone, and caSMCs failed to differentiate in Notch3-null hearts.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A,B

claim: caSMCs failed to differentiate in Notch3-null hearts.
source: The Jagged-1 ligand Notch3 was upregulated in pericytes at the arterial remodeling zone, and caSMCs failed to differentiate in Notch3-null hearts.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Notch3-null mice shown in Figure 7

claim: A delay in smooth muscle differentiation in the absence of Notch3 and Jagged-1 has been observed in other organ systems.
source: A delay in smooth muscle differentiation in the absence of Notch3 and Jagged-1 has been observed in other organ systems (Briot et al., 2014; Doi et al., 2006; High et al., 2008; Hofmann et al., 2012; Jin et al., 2008; Manderfield et al., 2012; Yang and Proweller, 2011), however nothing is known about their roles in caSMC differentiation.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Nothing is known about the roles of Notch3 and Jagged-1 in caSMC differentiation.
source: A delay in smooth muscle differentiation in the absence of Notch3 and Jagged-1 has been observed in other organ systems (Briot et al., 2014; Doi et al., 2006; High et al., 2008; Hofmann et al., 2012; Jin et al., 2008; Manderfield et al., 2012; Yang and Proweller, 2011), however nothing is known about their roles in caSMC differentiation.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study

claim: This study is the first to show the importance of Notch3 signaling in stimulating the pericyte to smooth muscle transition.
source: Furthermore, due to the previous lack of knowledge of the lineage relationship between pericytes and smooth muscle cells, we are the first to show the importance of Notch3 signaling in stimulating the pericyte to smooth muscle transition.
evidence: This is a summary statement of a primary finding of the study

claim: Jagged-1 and Notch signaling has been reported to be upregulated by sheer stress in vitro.
source: Jagged-1 and Notch signaling has been reported to be upregulated by sheer stress in vitro(McCormick et al., 2001; Theodoris et al., 2015), and we provide evidence that this occurs in vivo following coronary plexus attachment to the aorta.
evidence: Supported by citations to McCormick et al., 2001 and Theodoris et al., 2015

claim: Jagged-1 upregulation occurs in vivo following coronary plexus attachment to the aorta.
source: Jagged-1 and Notch signaling has been reported to be upregulated by sheer stress in vitro(McCormick et al., 2001; Theodoris et al., 2015), and we provide evidence that this occurs in vivo following coronary plexus attachment to the aorta.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in wild type and Isl1 mutant hearts

claim: Epicardial cells differentiate into Notch3low pericytes that cover the entire coronary plexus as it populates the myocardium.
source: Together, our data support a working model (Figure 9) where epicardial cells differentiate into Notch3low pericytes that cover the entire coronary plexus as it populates the myocardium.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the collective findings of the study

claim: Pericytes located on plexus vessels that receive blood flow-induced Jagged-1 upregulate Notch3 and differentiate into caSMCs.
source: Then, the pericytes located on plexus vessels that receive blood flow-induced Jagged-1 upregulate Notch3 and differentiate into caSMCs.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the collective findings of the study

claim: Blood flow initiation is correlated with molecular changes that mark the site of arterial development in the coronary vascular plexus.
source: Thus, blood flow initiation is correlated with molecular changes that mark the site of arterial development in the coronary vascular plexus and may stimulate vessel remodeling and pericyte differentiation into smooth muscle.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between blood flow initiation and Jagged-1 expression

claim: Blood flow initiation may stimulate vessel remodeling and pericyte differentiation into smooth muscle.
source: Thus, blood flow initiation is correlated with molecular changes that mark the site of arterial development in the coronary vascular plexus and may stimulate vessel remodeling and pericyte differentiation into smooth muscle.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed correlations

claim: Studies dissecting the role of PDGFRs, TCF21, and Myocardin-Related Transcription Factors have provided evidence that the decision to differentiate into either the cardiac fibroblast or caSMC lineage occurs in epicardial cells at the heart's surface.
source: Studies dissecting the role of PDGFRs, TCF21, and Myocardin-Related Transcription Factors have provided evidence that the decision to differentiate into either the cardiac fibroblast or caSMC lineage occurs in epicardial cells at the heart's surface (Acharya et al., 2012; Braitsch et al., 2012; Mellgren, et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2011; Trembley et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Progression down the caSMC lineage occurs early in development, mostly between e10.5 and 12.5.
source: In addition, progression down the caSMC lineage occurs early in development, mostly between e10.5 and 12.5 (Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wei et al., 2015

claim: Endothelial cells migrating directly beneath the epicardium at e10.5-12.5 acquire pericytes.
source: We show that endothelial cells migrating directly beneath the epicardium at this time point acquire pericytes and pericytes within caSMC containing clones are usually located near the heart's surface as well as deeper layers.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: Pericytes within caSMC containing clones are usually located near the heart's surface as well as deeper layers.
source: We show that endothelial cells migrating directly beneath the epicardium at this time point acquire pericytes and pericytes within caSMC containing clones are usually located near the heart's surface as well as deeper layers.
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A

claim: Migrating coronary vessels could trigger adjacent epicardial cells to differentiate into pericytes at the surface and support their movement into the myocardium along with invading endothelial cells.
source: Thus, migrating coronary vessels could trigger adjacent epicardial cells to differentiate into pericytes at the surface and support their movement into the myocardium along with invading endothelial cells.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the observed spatial relationships

claim: The subset of pericytes that traveled to arterializing vessels receives signals to become caSMCs.
source: Then, the subset of these pericytes that traveled to arterializing vessels receives signals to become caSMCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the clonal analysis and Notch3 signaling data

claim: Clones generally segregated between those containing pericytes/caSMCs and those with other cell types not positive for cell type specific markers, likely fibroblasts.
source: Clones also generally segregated between those containing pericytes/caSMCs and those with other cell types not positive for our cell type specific markers, likely fibroblasts, the latter of which did not integrate into the smooth muscle layer even when directly adjacent to the artery.
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Two different epicardial derived pathways diverge at the surface of the heart where the pericyte/caSMC lineage travels along vessels as they invade the myocardium.
source: Together, these findings provide strong evidence that two different epicardial derived pathways diverge at the surface of the heart where the pericyte/caSMC lineage travels along vessels as they invade the myocardium to provide the different mural cells of the coronary vasculature.
evidence: This is inferred from the clonal analysis data showing segregation of cell types

claim: Embryonic pericytes within caSMC clones were not merely an intermediate cell type that is depleted during development.
source: This suggests that embryonic pericytes within caSMC clones were not merely an intermediate cell type that is depleted during development, but that cells not differentiating remain and function as cardiac pericytes throughout life.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of pericyte-caSMC clones in adult hearts

claim: Cells not differentiating into caSMCs remain and function as cardiac pericytes throughout life.
source: This suggests that embryonic pericytes within caSMC clones were not merely an intermediate cell type that is depleted during development, but that cells not differentiating remain and function as cardiac pericytes throughout life.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of pericyte-caSMC clones in adult hearts

claim: Pericytes travel very little along a vessel once they establish their location during development.
source: The tight clustering in adult hearts also indicate that pericytes travel very little along a vessel once they establish their location during development, at least in this organ.
evidence: This is inferred from the tight clustering of labeled cells in adult hearts

claim: The embryonic heart appears to have developed an efficient method of distributing smooth muscle progenitors.
source: Thus, the embryonic heart appears to have developed an efficient method of distributing smooth muscle progenitors, cells that our data suggests maintain their cell-type specific function as pericytes at vessels that do not receive arterial blood flow and differentiation signals.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings

claim: Studies in the adult heart and other adult tissues report that perivascular cells are a heterogeneous population with mesenchymal stem cell properties that can contribute to tissue fibrosis.
source: Studies in the adult heart and other adult tissues report that perivascular cells are a heterogeneous population with mesenchymal stem cell properties that can contribute to tissue fibrosis (Chen et al., 2015; Ding et al., 2012; Kramann et al., 2014; Dulauroy et al., 2012; Stallcup, 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Epicardial-derived cells at the coronary artery remodeling zone were found to be almost exclusively either PDGFRβ+Notch3+NG2+PDGFRα- (pericytes) or PDGFRβ-Notch3-PDGFRα+ (fibroblasts).
source: Because a large number of caSMCs arise from the epicardium, we characterized epicardial-derived cells at the coronary artery remodeling zone. These were found to be almost exclusively either PDGFRβ+Notch3+NG2+PDGFRα- (pericytes) or PDGFRβ-Notch3-PDGFRα+ (fibroblasts) suggesting less heterogeneity in the epicardial-derived cellular compartment at this age.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 2L

claim: There is less heterogeneity in the epicardial-derived cellular compartment during development.
source: These were found to be almost exclusively either PDGFRβ+Notch3+NG2+PDGFRα- (pericytes) or PDGFRβ-Notch3-PDGFRα+ (fibroblasts) suggesting less heterogeneity in the epicardial-derived cellular compartment at this age.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that epicardial-derived cells at the remodeling zone are predominantly pericytes or fibroblasts

claim: The cellular milieu is likely more complex in the adult when immunity is active.
source: This could be due to development being an early and protected stage in the animal's life or that the cellular milieu is more complex in the adult when immunity is active.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences between development and adulthood

claim: Additional complexity is likely induced in tissue injury models.
source: Additional complexity is likely induced in tissue injury models.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about tissue injury models

source: In fact, developmental studies have show that an unidentified compensatory progenitor can provide caSMC if the epicardium is inhibited, although this source predisposes the arteries to disease (Smith et al., 2011; Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 2011 and Wei et al., 2015

claim: The compensatory caSMC source predisposes the arteries to disease.
source: In fact, developmental studies have show that an unidentified compensatory progenitor can provide caSMC if the epicardium is inhibited, although this source predisposes the arteries to disease (Smith et al., 2011; Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 2011 and Wei et al., 2015

claim: The description of pericytes as progenitors and their presence in the adult identifies the possibility that they could be utilized to produce new caSMCs during CA regeneration.

evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications

claim: Epicardial cells do not enter the adult heart, even after myocardial infarction.
source: Identifying the cellular pathway between the epicardium and smooth muscle is therefore important, particularly since it is known that epicardial cells do not enter the adult heart, even after myocardial infarction (Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2011

claim: Pericytes could be targeted without relying on the original progenitors (epicardial cells) being transported to form new collateral arteries.
source: Our data showing that pericytes are coronary artery smooth muscle progenitors and that they persist in the adult present the possibility that pericytes could be targeted without relying on the original progenitors (epicardial cells) being transported to form new collateral arteries.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic strategies
